n: The famine God foretold grows severe; Abraham’s brother Haran dies, while their father Terah remains alive in Ur. Hardship sets the stage for the family’s departure.
Abraham marries Sarai, and his brother Nahor marries Milcah, the daughter of their late brother Haran — keeping the family close-knit.
Abraham recalls the Lord’s earlier command: leave your country, your relatives, and your father’s house for a land God will show you. Faith often begins with leaving the familiar behind.

f.w: get thee out of thy country

n: Abraham leaves Ur for Canaan, taking his nephew Lot, Lot’s wife, and Sarai. His father Terah follows, and they stop at a place they name Haran — perhaps after Abraham’s deceased brother.
The famine ends, and Terah decides to stay in Haran because of its rich pastures — and because he returns to idolatry. Abraham’s father does not complete the journey of faith.
Abraham and Lot pray, and the Lord appears, telling Abraham to take Lot and leave Haran. Abraham will be God’s minister in a land his descendants will inherit forever — on condition that they obey.

f.w: when they hearken to my voice

n: The Lord describes His power: heaven is His home, earth His footstool, the sea obeys Him, and wind and fire serve as His chariot. The God who calls Abraham can keep His promises.

f.w: the wind and the fire to be my chariot

n: The Lord again reveals His name, Jehovah, and declares that He knows the end from the beginning. Because He sees all, Abraham can trust His protection.

f.w: I know the end from the beginning

n: The heart of the Abrahamic covenant: Abraham will become a great nation, be richly blessed, and his descendants will carry the gospel ministry and priesthood to every nation.

f.w: bear this ministry and Priesthood unto all nations

n: Everyone who receives the gospel will be counted as Abraham’s seed and bless him as their father. Covenant identity, not just bloodline, makes someone part of Abraham’s family.

God promises blessings to those who bless Abraham, and that all families of the earth will be blessed through his priesthood and literal descendants — with the blessings of the gospel and eternal life.

f.w: I will bless them that bless thee
all the families of the earth be blessed

n: After the Lord withdraws, Abraham reflects with joy: he had earnestly sought God, and now he has found Him.
Abraham remembers how God’s angel saved him from the idolatrous priests and resolves to obey and depart in peace.
Abraham leaves Haran as commanded, with Lot. Here he is said to be 62 years old; Genesis 12:4 gives 75, a difference that has been discussed but not definitively resolved.

f.g: Genesis 12:4 gives Abraham’s age as 75 when leaving Haran.

n: Abraham takes Sarai, Lot, their possessions, and the “souls” they had won in Haran — converts or household members who joined them — and they travel as tent-dwellers toward Canaan.

f.w: the souls that we had won in Haran
f.g: Likely people converted to the Lord or joined to their household (compare Genesis 12:5, “the souls that they had gotten”).

n: Living in tents, Abraham found that eternity itself — God — was their shelter, rock, and salvation as they traveled through Jershon toward Canaan.

f.g: A place on the route to Canaan, known only from this record (unrelated to the Book of Mormon land of Jershon).

n: In Jershon, Abraham builds an altar, offers sacrifice, and prays that the famine would spare his father’s household — showing love for the family that once tried to harm him.
They pass on to Shechem (“Sechem”) in the plains of Moreh, entering Canaanite territory. Surrounded by idolatry, Abraham prays devoutly and offers sacrifice.

f.g: Shechem, near modern Nablus in the central hill country (Genesis 12:6).
Hebrew, possibly “teacher”; Genesis 12:6 mentions “the plain [or oak] of Moreh.”

n: In answer to his prayers the Lord appears again and promises this land to Abraham’s descendants.

f.w: Unto thy seed will I give this land

n: Abraham moves to a mountain between Bethel and Hai (Ai), pitches his tent, builds another altar, and calls on the Lord. Wherever he settled, he made a place to worship.

f.g: Hebrew “house of God,” a site north of Jerusalem later important to Jacob (Genesis 28:19).
Ai, a town east of Bethel (Genesis 12:8; Joshua 7:2).

n: Abraham keeps moving south, but the famine continues and grows severe, so he decides to go down to Egypt temporarily.

f.g: to stay temporarily as a foreigner.

n: As they approach Egypt, the Lord warns Abraham that Sarai’s beauty will attract attention.
The Lord explains the danger: Egyptians who learn she is his wife may kill Abraham to take her.
The Lord instructs that Sarai should say she is Abraham’s sister so his life will be spared. Genesis 20:12 notes she was in fact his half-sister; here the instruction comes directly from God.
Abraham shares the Lord’s instructions with Sarai and asks for her help. Their lives depend on trusting God and each other in a dangerous foreign land.

f.w: my soul shall live because of thee
